did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ezekiel sees twenty-five men at the eastern gate of the house of the LORD, including Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, who are described as leaders of the people.
Did you know? The leaders of Jerusalem use the image of a pot and meat to express their confidence in the city: in their view, the city will protect them, and disaster is not near.
Did you know? The LORD declares that he knows the thoughts and deeds of the spirit of the people of Jerusalem, even when they try to justify their ways.

Did you know? The LORD turns the leaders’ pot metaphor against them: the slain people they killed are the “meat,” while the leaders themselves will be brought out of the city and will not enjoy its protection.
Did you know? When Pelatiah son of Benaiah dies in the prophetic vision, Ezekiel falls facedown and cries out to the LORD, fearing that he will completely destroy the remnant of Israel.
Did you know? Although the Israelites are scattered among the nations, the LORD says that he himself is a “sanctuary” for them in the lands to which they have gone.
Did you know? The chapter describes a profound inner transformation: the LORD promises to give the people “one heart,” a new spirit, and a heart of flesh instead of a heart of stone.
Did you know? The purpose of the new heart and new spirit is that the people will follow the LORD’s statutes, keep his judgments, and be his people, while he will be their God.
Did you know? At the end of the chariot vision, the glory of the LORD leaves the midst of the city and stands on the mountain east of it, signifying the glory’s departure from Jerusalem.
Did you know? After the spirit brings Ezekiel back to the exiles in Babylon, he tells them everything the LORD had shown him about Jerusalem and Israel’s future.
